text: High, Medium, Low versus an actual dollar figure — qualitative and quantitative risk assessment get treated like the easy version and the hard version of the same task, but that's not really right. They answer two different questions, and this lesson is about knowing which one you're actually asking before you pick a method.

Qualitative assessment answers: of everything on our plate, what should we work on first? It usually comes straight from the likelihood times impact matrix from the last lesson. Quantitative assessment answers a different question entirely: is this specific risk worth spending this specific amount of money to reduce? That one gets answered in dollars, as an estimated annual loss exposure, not a category label.

Qualitative scoring is fast — a workshop of security staff and stakeholders can score fifty risks in an afternoon using nothing but judgment. The cost is subjectivity. High means something different to the engineer who's watched a system fail before and the executive who's only read about it in a briefing. Because the scores share no common unit, a High in one team's register can't be meaningfully compared to a High in another team's.

Quantitative assessment fixes that by denominating every risk in dollars — something like four hundred thousand to two point one million in expected annual loss, with a median around nine hundred thousand. Because it's the same unit every time, a ransomware scenario and a regulatory fine scenario can be stacked directly against each other, and against the cost of the control that would reduce them. That rigor costs real time and data, so it gets reserved for decisions big enough to deserve it: an insurance renewal, a board asking for a dollar figure, an expensive buy-versus-build call.

The two aren't competitors. Run qualitative scoring continuously to narrow a two-hundred-item register down to the ten or so that actually matter, then spend the quantitative effort only on that short list before real money gets committed. Next lesson covers FAIR, the published model most organizations actually use to run that quantitative pass in a structured, repeatable way instead of guessing a dollar figure from scratch.
